title: In England, efforts to save a vanishing heritage – 9 strings at a time
text:
In England, efforts to save a vanishing heritage – 9 strings at a time
Fans of puppet shows are trying to save the traditional art of marionette-making in the United Kingdom before the skills are lost.
Sitting in an historic temperance hall-turned-puppet-theater in North London, Jasmine Chiu recounts the horror of being asked, midperformance, to fetch a pair of scissors so that a hopelessly tangled marionette could be snipped.
“At first, I was like, ‘No! I’m not going to bring the scissors!’” the professional dancer, actor, and performer recounts. But it turned out to be the right move, she says, and the first of many moments where she learned how to make a quick fix in front of an audience she couldn’t even see.
“I’m the kind of person who wants to be good at what they do immediately,” she says, with a laugh. “And the marionettes were really humbling. ... It’s very technical, actually.”
Puppet shows have been popular in the United Kingdom for hundreds of years. But now, only a handful of traditional marionette-makers remain. Efforts are underway to rekindle this fading heritage before their skills are lost.
In under two months this year, Ms. Chiu and five other accomplished performers took on a daunting task: Help preserve an endangered British heritage art by putting on a marionette show, despite never having held such a puppet.
The marionettes – or puppets – come in all shapes and sizes, many crafted from wood; some depict humans, others fantastical creatures, all intricately and lovingly made.
The show, “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice,” became a battle cry at London’s historic Little Angel Theatre in August to restore a dying genre of performance in a country that is believed to have only five or fewer full-time professional marionette-makers left. In 2023, Heritage Craft added marionette-making to its list of endangered trades, and British university degrees dedicated to making the string puppets no longer exist.
Marionettes “tap into British culture” and are “an absolute joy,” says Oliver Hymans, a seasoned puppeteer and the associate director of Little Angel Theatre. During the pandemic, he found himself with time to explore marionette theater in depth, learning how to carve them under a master and researching their heritage.
“I’d done every type of puppetry, but never string puppets, and I had always seen these beautiful marionettes hanging backstage and these mysterious hand controls,” Mr. Hymans says. Quickly he realized how few people are still making them. Even fewer are performing with them.
Italian puppeteers brought marionettes to Britain in the 17th century. But, in fact, British puppetry had taken off well before that. Shows are believed to go back 600 years and were given a boost during the Puritan Revolution of the mid-1600s, when the government banned most traditional theaters from using live actors. It drove some performers to use puppets in street performances instead.
“Plays and frivolities were banned, but puppet shows were too lowly a form to make it into the official proscriptions and escaped banning,” says Glyn Edwards, a longtime puppeteer and “Punch and Judy” performer.
During the Victorian era, puppets further flourished as “an art form suitable for the working classes,” Mr. Hymans says. In the second half of the 18th century, 29 puppet theaters dotted London alone, according to historians.
Those who grew up in the U.K. between the 1940s and 1960s also became familiar with British marionettes through the hit children’s TV programs “Bill and Ben,” “Muffin the Mule,” and “Thunderbirds.”
In recent years, large theater productions such as “War Horse,” “Life of Pi,” and “The Lion King” have demonstrated that other forms of puppetry are still in fashion.
But overall, traveling marionette troops have declined in recent decades, seeing fewer opportunities in vaudeville and variety theater. As the industry has slowly died out, so has the demand for skills such as marionette-making or operating the complex puppets.
“Marionettes are complicated constructions and don’t travel simply and easily,” according to Mr. Edwards. But passing on marionette skills are important “so that they are not lost to future generations,” he says.
Back at Little Angel Theatre, Ms. Chiu climbs the creaky wooden steps to the marionette bridge backstage, where she and other performers stand elevated out of sight, as they work the hidden puppet controls. Founded in 1961 by a puppeteer who acquired a former Victorian temperance hall damaged during the Blitz of World War II, the theater holds one of the world’s last remaining double marionette bridges, suitable for long-string puppets. These have two connected walkways in a U-shape to allow more puppeteers to move and work.
“Up on the bridge, there’s just these old pieces of paper – these notes from like 1983, you know? You can feel the history of it,” says Ms. Chiu. “Now that I have honestly fallen in love with [marionettes], I do feel a sense of responsibility – a desire – to keep them alive.”
Mr. Hymans, enthusiastically going over the bridge’s recent restoration, speaks about the importance of passing on the torch.
“There’s no other place in Britain like this,” he says, with a grin, at one point bumping his head into some hanging string puppets as he emerges from underneath the stage to show some of its original timber. “The whole point of marionettes is that they’re designed to be performed. They’re a part of our living heritage.”
